title: Retrieve What Helps, Only When It Helps: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Selective Retrieval-Augmented Machine Translation

paper.title:
Retrieve What Helps, Only When It Helps:
Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Selective
Retrieval-Augmented Machine Translation
paper.abstract: Abstract Retrieving external knowledge can improve large language model (LLM) translation by providing supplementary information such as idiom interpretations and terminology. However, existing retrieval-augmented machine translation systems typically apply predefined retrieval strategies uniformly across all inputs. We argue that translation operates in a partial-evidence regime: LLM’s parametric knowledge suffices for many inputs, while external evidence benefits a subset and usually supports rather than directly provides the desired translation. This creates two challenges: deciding when to retrieve and what evidence to acquire. We introduce Selective Retrieval-Augmented Translation ( SRAT ), an agentic reinforcement learning framework that learns when to translate directly or retrieve, what to retrieve, and how to integrate these decisions by optimizing final translation quality. To align evidence retrieval with downstream translation quality rather than simple semantic similarity, we further develop joint Plackett–Luce optimization and translation-quality contrastive training for retriever-training. Experiments on idiom, knowledge-intensive, and document-level translation with offline or online retrieval show that SRAT consistently outperforms never- and always-retrieve baselines, and quality-aligned retriever training provides further gains when similarity-based retrieval is insufficient. The results demonstrate the benefit of treating retrieval as a learnable translation action rather than fixed preprocessing.

The results demonstrate the benefit of treating retrieval as a learnable translation action rather than fixed preprocessing. 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) have become strong general-purpose machine translation (MT) systems, particularly after multilingual instruction tuning and translation-specific adaptation ( Jiao et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2024 ) . In particular, recent LLMs demonstrate strong ability to interpret contextual cues and leverage external knowledge. These capabilities have motivated retrieval-augmented MT systems that provide bilingual examples, idiom definitions, terminology, or supporting documents to further support and improve translation quality ( Li et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025b ) . Figure 1: SRAT’s workflow by integrating reasoning, retrieval, and translation for LLM-based translation. However, recent studies ( Sun et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) have shown that retrieval is not uniformly beneficial for translation. Existing retrieval-augmented MT pipelines typically apply a predefined retrieval strategy: retrieve for every input with a heuristic, similarity-based matching rule. This overlooks a fundamental gap in LLM-based translation: for some inputs, the model’s parametric knowledge is already sufficient, while for others, external evidence such as idiom interpretations, canonical entities, technical terms, or background knowledge can be crucial. Moreover, heuristic, similarity-based retrieval can provide no help and even introduce noisy or misleading context that distracts the model and degrades an otherwise correct translation ( Sun et al., 2026 ) . For example, a semantically close document may merely repeat query terms without providing actionable knowledge, while a more distant one may contain exactly the idiom interpretation, entity convention, or background knowledge the translation requires. Translation therefore differs from answer-oriented retrieval settings, in which a relevant document often directly contains the evidence needed to produce the final response. We refer to this setting as the partial-evidence regime, which captures two properties of retrieval in MT. First, external evidence is beneficial for only a subset of inputs where the model’s parametric knowledge doesn’t suffices. Second, when evidence is needed, retrieval based solely on semantic similarity may fail to surface the most useful evidence. This raises two learning problems. The first is retrieval adaptivity : the model must determine when additional evidence is useful instead of retrieving by default. The second is retrieval quality alignment : once retrieval is invoked, the system must determine what evidence actually improves the final translation quality. To address them, we propose Selective Retrieval-Augmented Translation ( SRAT ), an agentic reinforcement-learning framework that treats reasoning, retrieval, and translation as actions in a unified policy. Given a source input, the model’s action space at each step includes reasoning about the translation, generating a retrieval query and incorporating the returned evidence, or terminating with the final translation. Rather than supervising which examples should retrieve, we optimize complete trajectories using final translation quality. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( Shao et al., 2024 ) allows trajectories with different retrieval decisions and queries to compete for the same input, thereby learning when retrieval is worthwhile and what to retrieve to improve final translation quality. Moreover, we develop two approaches for further aligning the retriever with downstream translation quality rather than simple semantic similarity. First, a natural and principled approach is to jointly optimize the LLM translator and retriever end-to-end. To achieve it, we replace deterministic top- k k selection during training with a Plackett–Luce ranking policy ( Plackett, 1975 ) , whose selection log-probability allows trajectory-level translation reward to update the retriever through a score-function gradient. However, this joint signal can be noisy: a trajectory contains many LLM policy decisions but only a few retrieval actions, making credit assignment to the retriever inherently high-variance. To address this, we further introduce translation-quality contrastive training, which fixes the translator, evaluates candidate retrieval evidence by their measured effect on translation quality, and converts these into direct contrastive supervision. This isolates the effect of retrieval from other policy decisions, providing the retriever with substantially more targeted training signals. We evaluate SRAT across three translation settings: idiom translation, knowledge-intensive translation, and document-level translation. The first two use offline retrieval corpora, while the document-level setting additionally evaluates SRAT with online retrieval. Across these settings, SRAT consistently outperforms never-retrieve and always-retrieve baselines, demonstrating the benefit of learning when to retrieve and what evidence to seek. Ablations show that quality-aligned retriever training provides further significant gains when similarity-based retrieval is insufficient. We also find that the retrieval policy can be optimized with a frontier black-box translator, outperforming its direct translation and indicating that the adaptive retrieval decision training can be decoupled from the translator and optimized as a modular component for external generation models. Our main contributions are threefold: • Selective retrieval as a translation decision. We characterize LLM-based RAG translation as a partial-evidence regime in which external knowledge is useful only conditionally. We formulate machine translation by LLM as a sequential policy over reasoning, retrieval, and final translation, enabling the model to learn when and what to retrieve from translation outcomes rather than fixed routing rules. • Quality-aligned evidence retrieval. We propose two retriever-training strategies. Joint Plackett–Luce policy-gradient training propagates trajectory-level translation reward to evidence retrieval, while translation-quality contrastive training derives direct retriever supervision from controlled retrieval evidence interventions. Both align the retriever toward the downstream effect of retrieved evidence on translation quality rather than semantic similarity alone. • Evaluation across retrieval regimes. Experiments on idiom, knowledge-intensive, and document-level translation with offline and online retrieval consistently outperform fixed never- and always-retrieve strategies. The results further show that quality-aligned retrieval is significantly beneficial when similarity-based retrieval is insufficient, and that adaptive retrieval policy learning can be decoupled from the translator to improve frontier black-box models beyond their direct translation performance. 2 Related Work Large Language Models for Translation. Early studies showed that general-purpose LLMs can deliver competitive translation performance, although results vary across languages, domains, and prompting strategies ( Jiao et al., 2023 ; Hendy et al., 2023 ) . Translation-specific continued pretraining and supervised fine-tuning further improve smaller open models; ALMA, for example, combines monolingual adaptation with high-quality parallel data ( Xu et al., 2024 ) . These efforts improve the underlying translator, but largely leave inference-time information acquisition outside the modeling problem. A parallel line of work introduces explicit deliberation into LLM-based MT. MAPS elicits multiple translation-relevant analyses before selecting among candidate outputs ( He et al., 2024 ) ; TEaR adopts a translate–estimate–refine procedure ( Feng et al., 2025 ) ; and DRT distills extended reasoning traces for figurative text ( Wang et al., 2025a ) . These studies suggest that additional computation can help difficult inputs, but the form and amount are typically fixed in advance. SRAT instead learns when extra reasoning and retrieval really help for translation. Retrieval-Augmented Machine Translation. Retrieval has long been used in MT through translation memories and nearest-neighbor examples, while recent LLM-based systems draw on broader forms of external evidence. IdiomKB retrieves explanatory knowledge for idiomatic translation ( Li et al., 2024 ) , RAGtrans incorporates multilingual unstructured documents ( Wang et al., 2025b ) , and cross-cultural MT has explored multilingual knowledge graphs ( Conia and others, 2024 ) . These results demonstrate the value of external knowledge when the source alone is insufficient. Yet most systems either retrieve by default or rely on predefined routing, while retrieval is often optimized separately from the final translation objective. Our focus is instead on whether retrieved evidence improves translation quality for a given input and model state. Adaptive Retrieval and Reinforcement Learning. Adaptive retrieval has been studied mainly in language modeling and question answering. FLARE triggers retrieval when generation becomes uncertain ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) ; Self-RAG learns retrieval and reflection actions from supervised preference data ( Asai et al., 2024 ) ; and Search-R1 uses reinforcement learning to acquire multi-turn search-and-reason behavior from answer-level rewards ( Jin and others, 2025 ) . These works show that retrieval can be integrated into a learned generation policy.
